parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: In the Hafele–Keating experiment, a clock was flown around the world. Using special relativity, discuss how its motion affects the time registered by the clock compared with a clock remaining on Earth’s surface.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: In a laboratory, a moving electron takes 29.8 ns to travel from a detector to a target. Is the proper time between these two events less than, equal to, or greater than 29.8 ns? Explain.

answer.text: Less than 29.8 ns. The two events occur at the same place in the electron’s rest frame, so that frame measures proper time Δτ. Laboratory time is Δt = γΔτ, with γ > 1.

evidence.review: Worked answer checked against the source marking guidance; wording adapted for independent IB practice.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A proton travelling along a beamline has Lorentz factor γ = 2.00. Calculate its speed as a fraction of c, to three significant figures.

evidence.question: B10a

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A beamline has proper length 4.80 km. A proton travels along it with Lorentz factor γ = 2.00. Calculate the beamline length measured in the proton’s reference frame.

answer.text: The beamline moves in the proton frame, so L = L0/γ = 4.80/2.00 = 2.40 km.

ibd-a88908df340c714d-q6:a.hint: Identify the frame in which the two events happen at the same place. Its clock measures the proper time.
notes: Time dilation is Δt = γΔτ, with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). Proper time is measured by one clock present at both events.
Use distances and speeds measured in the same frame. If a journey time is L/v in the Earth frame, the travelling clock records that interval divided by γ.

ibd-a88908df340c714d-q6:b.i.hint: Check whether the axes are x and ct, then locate events whose coordinates you can transform.
notes: On a spacetime diagram, the moving frame axes are tilted, and their scale marks cannot be copied by ordinary perpendicular projection.
Use the Lorentz transformation or invariant interval to calibrate the moving axes. For coordinates x and ct, a light ray has slope ±1 in equally scaled axes.

ibd-a88908df340c714d-q6:b.ii.hint: Identify the emission and reception as two separate events. Write their time and position differences in the Earth frame before changing frames.
notes: Use Δt′ = γ(Δt − vΔx/c²) with γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). Keep the sign of the signal’s displacement: it travels back towards Earth.
The events occur at different locations in both frames. Do not assume that either interval is a proper time and apply Δt = γΔτ without checking.

notes: Proper time belongs to a clock present at both events in its own rest frame. Do not identify “proper” with the laboratory merely because laboratory instruments took the measurement.

notes: The Lorentz factor is dimensionless and at least one. For a massive particle, the resulting v/c must be below one.

cross-vc23-written-B10b:whole.hint: Identify the frame in which the beamline itself is at rest.
notes: Proper length is measured in the object’s rest frame. Contraction applies along the relative motion; it is not a change in the beamline’s own rest length.

ibd-a88908df340c714d-q6:b.ii.text: In the Earth frame the signal is emitted at (t = 50 y, x = 30 ly) and received at (t = 80 y, x = 0). Thus Δt = 30 y and Δx = −30 ly. With γ = 1.25, Δt′ = γ(Δt − vΔx/c²) = 1.25[30 − 0.60(−30)] = 60 years. The events occur at different positions, so a proper-time shortcut cannot be used for this interval.

ibd-7c37430fd5ce856d-q4:whole.text: The journey takes 2000/(0.98 × 3.0 × 10⁸) ≈ 6.8 μs in the ground frame. Without time dilation this is about three mean lifetimes, so only a small fraction would survive. Time dilation increases the mean lifetime in this frame to γτ₀ = 5.0 × 2.2 = 11 μs, allowing a much larger fraction to reach the ground. The observed number of muons supports the dilated lifetime; a mean lifetime is not a fixed expiry time for every particle.

ibd-b3e86d458430f237-q4:whole.text: Maxwell’s theory identifies light as an electromagnetic wave with a definite propagation speed in vacuum. Special relativity takes this vacuum speed c to be the same for every inertial observer, independently of the motion of the source. The electromagnetic laws therefore have the same form in all inertial frames.

ibd-10bb8b2b4d47787b-q17:whole.text: Considering motion alone, a clock moving at speed v in an inertial frame accumulates proper time dτ = dt/γ. A higher speed means a larger γ and less elapsed time on that clock. For aircraft and ground clocks, compare both speeds in the same inertial frame: their different speeds, including the effect of Earth’s rotation, produce different accumulated times. Eastward and westward journeys need not give the same comparison with the ground clock.
